module.title: Phase Equilibria & Transformations
module.intro: Materials are defined by their phases, and phases are defined by thermodynamics. This module covers how phase diagrams encode equilibrium, how new phases nucleate and grow, and how the transformations that produce real microstructures (solidification, precipitation, martensite, spinodal decomposition, ordering) actually work at the atomic scale.

articles.title: Unary & Binary Phase Diagrams
articles.description: Reading phase diagrams for one- and two-component systems, with the iron-carbon diagram as the central example.
articles.intro: A phase diagram is a map. It tells you which phases are stable at a given temperature, pressure and composition. Reading one fluently is perhaps the single most useful skill in physical metallurgy, and the iron-carbon diagram is the most important map in all of materials science.
body: Start simple. A single pure substance can exist as solid, liquid or gas. The unary phase diagram plots the regions of stability for each phase as a function of temperature and pressure. For pure iron at 1 atm, you heat through three solid phases before reaching the liquid: $\alpha$-Fe (BCC, stable to 912 °C), $\gamma$-Fe (FCC, 912 to 1394 °C), $\delta$-Fe (BCC, 1394 to 1538 °C), then liquid above 1538 °C. These are real numbers you should know.

The boundaries between single-phase regions are coexistence lines, where two phases exist together in equilibrium. Where three coexistence lines meet, you get a triple point: three phases in equilibrium at a unique temperature and pressure. Water's triple point is 0.01 °C, 611.7 Pa. Carbon's triple point (graphite/diamond/liquid) is near 4600 K and 12 GPa, which tells you how extreme the conditions need to be to melt diamond.
The Clausius-Clapeyron equation gives the slope of each coexistence line:

For most materials, melting increases volume ($\Delta V > 0$) and absorbs heat ($\Delta H > 0$), so the solid-liquid line slopes to the right: higher pressure raises the melting point. Water is the famous exception, because ice is less dense than liquid water. Its solid-liquid line slopes to the left. Iron's BCC-to-FCC transition at 912 °C also has a negative $\Delta V$ (FCC is denser), so the $\alpha/\gamma$ boundary tilts toward lower temperature under pressure.

Add a second component and you gain a composition axis. The diagram is now plotted as temperature vs composition (at fixed pressure, usually 1 atm). Every point in the diagram represents a specific temperature and overall composition. The diagram tells you three things: which phases are present, what their compositions are, and how much of each there is.

The simplest binary diagram is a lens-shaped two-phase region between a liquidus (upper curve) and a solidus (lower curve). The Cu-Ni system is close to this ideal. Copper melts at 1085 °C, nickel at 1455 °C. At any temperature between the two curves, liquid and solid coexist. The compositions of each phase are read from the horizontal endpoints of a tie line at that temperature. The relative amounts come from the lever rule (Article 7.2).

The Fe-C diagram is the single most referenced phase diagram in engineering. It governs the behaviour of every steel and cast iron ever made. The diagram is usually plotted to 6.67 wt% C, corresponding to the compound cementite, Fe₃C. Key features:
The $\gamma$ (austenite) field: FCC iron with up to 2.14 wt% C in solid solution at 1147 °C. This is the parent phase for almost all steel heat treatments.
The $\alpha$ (ferrite) field: BCC iron with very limited carbon solubility, maximum 0.022 wt% C at 727 °C. The low solubility of carbon in ferrite drives precipitation of cementite during cooling.
Cementite, Fe₃C: an orthorhombic compound at 6.67 wt% C. Hard, brittle, and the default carbide in plain carbon steels.
Three invariant reactions define the iron-carbon diagram. At each, three phases coexist at a single temperature and composition (zero degrees of freedom).

Eutectic (1147 °C, 4.30 wt% C): Liquid $\rightarrow$ $\gamma$ + Fe₃C. A liquid of eutectic composition solidifies directly into a two-phase mixture of austenite and cementite. Cast irons live near this composition. The eutectic structure (ledeburite) forms at a single temperature with no freezing range, which is why cast irons have good fluidity for casting.

Eutectoid (727 °C, 0.76 wt% C): $\gamma$ $\rightarrow$ $\alpha$ + Fe₃C. Austenite of eutectoid composition transforms on cooling into a lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite called pearlite. This is the reaction that makes medium-carbon steels useful. A 1080 steel (0.80 wt% C) is nearly eutectoid and transforms almost entirely to pearlite on slow cooling.

Peritectic (1495 °C, 0.17 wt% C): $\delta$ + Liquid $\rightarrow$ $\gamma$. A high-temperature reaction where delta-ferrite reacts with liquid to form austenite. Less commonly discussed than the eutectic and eutectoid, but it matters for continuous casting of low-carbon steels: the volume contraction at the peritectic causes uneven solidification and surface cracking.

Steels with less than 0.76 wt% C are hypoeutectoid. On slow cooling below the $A_3$ temperature, proeutectoid ferrite nucleates first at austenite grain boundaries, forming a white network in etched micrographs. The remaining austenite reaches 0.76 wt% C and transforms to pearlite at 727 °C. Hypereutectoid steels (above 0.76 wt% C) precipitate proeutectoid cementite first, then the remaining austenite again transforms to pearlite. The difference is visible under the microscope and determines mechanical properties: a 1045 steel is roughly half ferrite, half pearlite; a 1095 steel is almost entirely pearlite with thin cementite films on prior austenite boundaries.
Reading a binary diagram: a worked example

Consider a plain carbon steel with 0.40 wt% C, cooled slowly from 900 °C. At 900 °C the alloy is entirely austenite ($\gamma$). On cooling through the $A_3$ temperature (approximately 820 °C for this composition), it enters the $\alpha + \gamma$ two-phase field. Proeutectoid ferrite begins to form. As temperature falls, the ferrite fraction grows and the remaining austenite becomes enriched in carbon, following the $A_3$ line. At 727 °C, the remaining austenite (now at 0.76 wt% C) undergoes the eutectoid transformation to pearlite. The final microstructure is proeutectoid ferrite plus pearlite.
The fraction of proeutectoid ferrite is given by the lever rule at 728 °C (just above the eutectoid):
About half and half. This is consistent with the micrograph you would see: roughly equal areas of white ferrite and dark-etching pearlite.

The Fe-C diagram is not the only one worth knowing. The Cu-Sn system has a peritectic cascade and is the basis of bronze metallurgy. The Al-Si system has a simple eutectic at 12.6 wt% Si and 577 °C, central to aluminium casting alloys. The Cu-Zn system (brasses) shows order-disorder transitions at low zinc content and a cascade of intermediate phases at higher zinc. The Ti-Al system, with its ordered $\gamma$-TiAl intermetallic, is the basis of lightweight turbine blade alloys.
Every binary system encodes the thermodynamics of mixing between two elements. Learning to read these diagrams quickly and correctly is time well spent.

A plain carbon steel contains 0.20 wt% C and is cooled slowly from 900 °C to room temperature. Describe the sequence of phase transformations. Calculate the fraction of proeutectoid ferrite and the fraction of pearlite in the final microstructure.

At 900 °C, the alloy is single-phase austenite. On cooling through the $A_3$ line (roughly 850 °C for 0.20 wt% C), proeutectoid ferrite begins to precipitate from austenite grain boundaries. The remaining austenite becomes richer in carbon. At 727 °C, the austenite has reached 0.76 wt% C and undergoes the eutectoid reaction to form pearlite.
Fraction of proeutectoid ferrite (lever rule just above 727 °C):
The microstructure is about 76% proeutectoid ferrite and 24% pearlite. This is a low-carbon steel with considerable ductility: the ferrite fraction dominates.

articles.title: The Lever Rule & Phase Fractions
articles.description: Deriving the lever rule from mass conservation and applying it to calculate phase fractions in two-phase regions.
articles.intro: When an alloy sits inside a two-phase region on a binary phase diagram, you can read the compositions of the two phases from the endpoints of a tie line. But how much of each phase is present? The lever rule answers this, and it follows from nothing more than conservation of mass.
body: Pick a point inside any two-phase region on a binary diagram. Draw a horizontal line (isothermal) through it until it hits the phase boundaries on either side. This is a tie line. Its left endpoint gives the composition of one phase; its right endpoint gives the composition of the other. Every point along that tie line represents a different overall alloy composition, but the phase compositions are the same; only the relative amounts differ.

For example, in the Cu-Ni system at 1250 °C, a tie line in the liquid + solid region might run from 37 wt% Ni (liquid composition) to 50 wt% Ni (solid composition). An alloy of overall composition 42 wt% Ni at 1250 °C consists of liquid at 37 wt% Ni and solid at 50 wt% Ni, with the relative amounts determined by the lever rule.
The lever rule states that the fraction of each phase is inversely proportional to its distance from the overall composition on the tie line. It is a direct consequence of conservation of mass.
Let $C_0$ be the overall composition, $C_\alpha$ the composition of phase $\alpha$, and $C_\beta$ the composition of phase $\beta$. Let $f_\alpha$ and $f_\beta = 1 - f_\alpha$ be the mass fractions.
Conservation of the alloying element requires:

The fraction of each phase equals the length of the opposite arm of the tie line, divided by the total tie-line length. This is why it is called the lever rule: the overall composition is the fulcrum, and the two phases balance like weights on a lever.

A Cu-Ni alloy of overall composition 42 wt% Ni is held at 1250 °C, inside the two-phase (liquid + solid) field. At this temperature, the liquidus gives $C_L = 37$ wt% Ni and the solidus gives $C_S = 50$ wt% Ni.

The alloy is 38% solid and 62% liquid at this temperature. Notice that the overall composition (42 wt% Ni) is closer to the liquid composition (37 wt% Ni) than to the solid composition (50 wt% Ni), so there is more liquid than solid. The lever rule always works this way: the phase whose composition is closer to the overall composition is present in the larger amount.
Applying the lever rule across a cooling path

As an alloy cools through a two-phase region, the tie line changes: the phase compositions migrate along the liquidus and solidus curves, and the phase fractions change. Tracking the lever rule at successive temperatures gives you the solidification history.

Take a Cu-40 wt% Ni alloy cooling from the fully liquid state. At the liquidus temperature (about 1280 °C), the first solid appears with a composition near 52 wt% Ni, considerably richer in nickel than the liquid. As the temperature drops, the solid composition slides down the solidus, the liquid composition slides down the liquidus, and the solid fraction increases. At the solidus temperature (about 1220 °C), the last drop of liquid disappears and the alloy is fully solid.

If cooling is slow enough for diffusion to maintain equilibrium at every instant, the final solid is uniform at 40 wt% Ni. If cooling is too fast, the solid cores retain their early, nickel-rich composition while later-solidifying material is nickel-poor. This is coring, and it means the lever rule (which assumes equilibrium) overestimates the fraction of solid at any given temperature during non-equilibrium cooling.

The lever rule applies anywhere you have a two-phase field, not just during solidification. In the Fe-C system just above 727 °C, a hypoeutectoid steel with 0.40 wt% C sits in the $\alpha + \gamma$ field. The lever rule gives:
Just over half the alloy is austenite at 728 °C. That austenite will transform to pearlite on further cooling, so the alloy ends up roughly 51% pearlite.
Using the wrong denominator. The denominator is always the full length of the tie line ($C_\beta - C_\alpha$), not the distance from one end to the overall composition.

Applying the lever rule in a single-phase region. If the point lies in a single-phase field, the phase fraction is 1 and the composition of that phase equals the overall composition. There is no tie line.
Forgetting that the lever rule gives weight fractions if the diagram is in weight percent, and mole fractions if the diagram is in mole percent. Mixing the two will give wrong answers.

The lever rule gives weight (or mole) fractions, not volume fractions. When comparing to a micrograph, where you estimate area fractions by eye, you need volume fractions. Convert using the densities of each phase: $f^{\text{vol}}_\alpha = (f_\alpha / \rho_\alpha) \big/ (f_\alpha / \rho_\alpha + f_\beta / \rho_\beta)$. For ferrite ($\rho \approx 7.87$ g/cm$^3$) and cementite ($\rho \approx 7.69$ g/cm$^3$), the difference is small. For $\alpha$-Al and Si in an Al-Si eutectic, it is not: Si is denser (2.33 vs 2.70 g/cm$^3$ for Al), so the volume fraction of Si is slightly less than its weight fraction.

An Al-4.5 wt% Cu alloy is held at 550 °C in the $\alpha$ + $\theta$ (Al₂Cu) two-phase field. At this temperature, the maximum solid solubility of Cu in $\alpha$-Al is 1.5 wt% Cu, and $\theta$ has a fixed composition of 53.5 wt% Cu (stoichiometric Al₂Cu is 53.5 wt% Cu). Calculate the weight fractions of $\alpha$ and $\theta$.

The alloy is about 94.2% $\alpha$-Al and 5.8% $\theta$ (Al₂Cu) by weight. Even though the alloy contains 4.5 wt% Cu, the second phase is a small fraction because $\theta$ is very copper-rich (53.5 wt% Cu). A little $\theta$ goes a long way in accounting for the copper.

articles.title: Ternary Phase Diagrams
articles.description: How to read three-component phase diagrams: the Gibbs triangle, isothermal sections, liquidus projections and tie triangles.
articles.intro: Most engineering alloys contain three or more components. Representing the phase equilibria of a ternary system requires an equilateral triangle (the Gibbs triangle), and reading it correctly takes practice. The principles are the same as for binary diagrams, but the geometry is richer.
body: In a three-component system A-B-C, the composition space is two-dimensional. The Gibbs triangle maps it. Each vertex represents a pure component. Each edge is a binary system. Any point inside the triangle represents a ternary composition, and you read off the fraction of each component by measuring the perpendicular distance to the opposite edge (or equivalently, using the grid lines parallel to each edge).

The sum of the three components is always 100%. A point that lies 40% of the way from vertex B toward edge AC has 40% B. Its A and C fractions are read from the grid lines parallel to the BC and AB edges, respectively. This takes practice but becomes natural.

Temperature is the third axis, making the full ternary diagram a three-dimensional prism with the Gibbs triangle as the base and temperature as the vertical axis. This is difficult to visualise. In practice, we work with two-dimensional slices.

Cut the ternary prism at a fixed temperature and you get an isothermal section. It looks like the Gibbs triangle, now divided into single-phase, two-phase and three-phase regions. The rules are extensions of those for binary diagrams:
In a single-phase region, the alloy composition equals the phase composition.
In a two-phase region, pairs of conjugate phases are connected by tie lines. The lever rule applies along each tie line, just as in a binary.

In a three-phase region, the three phases have fixed compositions at the vertices of a tie triangle. Any overall composition inside that triangle has all three phases present, with fractions determined by the centre-of-gravity rule.

The key difference from binary diagrams: in a two-phase region, tie lines are not obvious from the diagram. They must be determined experimentally or calculated from thermodynamic models. You cannot simply draw a horizontal line; you must know the direction of the tie lines in that region.

Inside a three-phase triangle, the phase fractions are found by treating the overall composition as the centre of gravity of masses placed at the three vertices. If the overall composition $P$ lies at position $(x_P, y_P)$ inside a triangle with vertices at compositions $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, then the fraction of phase $\alpha$ is the area of the sub-triangle $P\beta\gamma$ divided by the total area of triangle $\alpha\beta\gamma$:
This reduces to the lever rule when one dimension is collapsed (i.e., in the binary limit).

The liquidus surface of the ternary prism, viewed from above, is projected onto the composition triangle. Isotherms (contour lines of equal temperature) show how the liquidus temperature varies with composition. Valleys between the primary solidification fields of different phases are called univariant lines (or monovariant troughs). Along these lines, liquid is in equilibrium with two solid phases. Where three univariant lines meet, you get a ternary invariant point, where liquid coexists with three solid phases.

The Al-Cu-Mg liquidus projection is essential for understanding 2xxx series aluminium alloys (such as 2024, the classic aerospace alloy). The primary $\alpha$-Al field dominates at low solute content, with univariant lines leading to ternary eutectics involving $\theta$ (Al₂Cu) and $S$ (Al₂CuMg). The ternary eutectic at roughly Al-33Cu-6Mg solidifies at about 507 °C.

A vertical section through the ternary prism, taken along a line across the Gibbs triangle, produces an isopleth. These look superficially like binary phase diagrams, but there is an important difference: tie lines generally do not lie in the plane of the section. You cannot apply the lever rule directly to an isopleth unless the tie lines happen to lie in that particular plane (which is rare).

Isopleths are useful for seeing phase fields and transformation temperatures along a particular composition path (for example, varying Cu content at fixed Mg/Al ratio), but quantitative phase-fraction calculations require the full isothermal section.

Real ternary systems are calculated using CALPHAD (Calculation of Phase Diagrams), which fits Gibbs energy models to experimental data and computes sections automatically. Software such as Thermo-Calc, PANDAT and FactSage generates isothermal sections, liquidus projections and property diagrams for any composition. The geometry described here is what you need to interpret the output.

Stainless steels are ternary (at minimum) alloys. The Fe-Cr-Ni isothermal section at 1100 °C shows three major phase fields: $\gamma$ (austenite), $\alpha$ (ferrite), and $\sigma$ (a brittle intermetallic). A standard 304 stainless (18 wt% Cr, 8 wt% Ni) sits firmly in the $\gamma$ field, which is why it is austenitic at service temperature. A lean duplex stainless (22 wt% Cr, 3 wt% Ni) sits in the $\alpha + \gamma$ two-phase field, giving a mixed ferritic-austenitic microstructure. The Schaeffler diagram, widely used in welding, is a simplified projection of this ternary phase equilibrium, using chromium and nickel equivalents to approximate the effect of additional alloying elements.

An alloy in a ternary system A-B-C has overall composition 30% A, 50% B, 20% C (all in wt%). At the temperature of interest, it lies inside a three-phase tie triangle with vertices at $\alpha$ (80% A, 10% B, 10% C), $\beta$ (5% A, 85% B, 10% C), and $\gamma$ (10% A, 10% B, 80% C). Calculate the phase fractions using a mass balance on any two components.
Set up mass balances on components A and B:
With the constraint $f_\alpha + f_\beta + f_\gamma = 1$, substitute $f_\gamma = 1 - f_\alpha - f_\beta$ into both equations:
30 = 80 f_\alpha + 5 f_\beta + 10(1 - f_\alpha - f_\beta) \implies 20 = 70 f_\alpha - 5 f_\beta
From the second: $f_\beta = 40/75 = 0.533$. Substituting into the first: $20 = 70 f_\alpha - 5(0.533)$, so $f_\alpha = (20 + 2.67)/70 = 0.324$. Then $f_\gamma = 1 - 0.324 - 0.533 = 0.143$.
The alloy is 32.4% $\alpha$, 53.3% $\beta$, 14.3% $\gamma$. The B-rich phase $\beta$ dominates, which makes sense given the high B content (50%) of the overall composition.

articles.title: Gibbs Phase Rule
articles.description: Counting degrees of freedom in multiphase, multicomponent systems, with worked examples from real phase diagrams.
articles.intro: How many variables can you independently change while maintaining a given set of phases in equilibrium? Gibbs answered this in 1876 with a rule so simple it fits in one line. It is the bookkeeping behind every phase diagram.
body: For a system with $C$ components and $P$ phases in equilibrium:

Here $F$ is the number of degrees of freedom: the number of intensive variables (temperature, pressure, phase compositions) you can independently vary without changing the number of phases present. The '2' counts temperature and pressure.
If pressure is fixed (the usual case for condensed-matter problems), the rule becomes:
The phase rule follows from counting equations and unknowns in the equilibrium conditions.

To specify the state of each phase, you need $C - 1$ independent composition variables per phase (mole fractions sum to 1), plus $T$ and $P$. With $P$ phases, the total number of intensive variables is $P(C - 1) + 2$.

Equilibrium requires that the chemical potential of each component is the same in every phase. For component $i$: $\mu_i^{(1)} = \mu_i^{(2)} = \dots = \mu_i^{(P)}$. That gives $P - 1$ equations per component, and $C$ components, so $C(P - 1)$ constraint equations total.
The degrees of freedom are the variables minus the constraints:
These examples all assume constant pressure ($F = C - P + 1$), with $C = 2$ (Fe and C).
Single-phase region (e.g., austenite): $F = 2 - 1 + 1 = 2$. You can vary both temperature and composition independently while remaining in the $\gamma$ field. This is an area on the diagram.
Two-phase region (e.g., $\alpha + \gamma$): $F = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$. Fixing the temperature fixes the compositions of both phases (the tie-line endpoints). This is a region bounded by two curves.

Three-phase equilibrium (e.g., the eutectoid: $\gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \text{Fe}_3\text{C}$): $F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$. Zero degrees of freedom. This is an invariant point: the temperature (727 °C), the austenite composition (0.76 wt% C), the ferrite composition (0.022 wt% C), and the cementite composition (6.67 wt% C) are all fixed. On the diagram, it is a horizontal line.
Why water has a triple point

For pure water ($C = 1$) at the triple point where solid, liquid and gas coexist ($P = 3$): $F = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0$. Zero degrees of freedom. The triple point occurs at exactly one temperature (273.16 K) and one pressure (611.7 Pa). You cannot change either variable without losing a phase. This is why the triple point of water is used as a thermometric fixed point: it is reproducible to any desired precision because equilibrium demands it occur at a unique $(T, P)$.

With three components ($C = 3$) at constant pressure, $F = 3 - P + 1 = 4 - P$. A single phase has $F = 3$: you can vary temperature and two composition variables. A two-phase field has $F = 2$: a two-dimensional area on the isothermal section. A three-phase field has $F = 1$: a fixed triangle at a given temperature, but the triangle can change with temperature. A four-phase equilibrium ($F = 0$) is invariant: it occurs at a single temperature, and all four phase compositions are fixed.

In most materials science problems, we work at atmospheric pressure and are interested only in solid and liquid phases (vapour is either absent or irrelevant). The effective phase rule is $F = C - P + 1$. Be explicit about this assumption. If the gas phase matters (e.g., in oxidation, carbothermic reduction, CVD), you must include it as a phase and use the full rule with '+2'.
The phase rule as a design tool

The phase rule is not just for interpreting diagrams. It constrains what is thermodynamically possible. If you want to heat-treat a ternary alloy and maintain three specific phases in equilibrium, you have $F = 3 - 3 + 1 = 1$ degree of freedom at constant pressure. You can choose the temperature, but then all three phase compositions are fixed. You cannot independently adjust both temperature and a phase composition. This limits your control. If you add a fourth component (making it a quaternary alloy), $F = 4 - 3 + 1 = 2$: now you can adjust temperature and one composition independently. Adding components increases design freedom, which is one reason modern superalloys contain ten or more elements.

In the Cu-Zn binary system at constant pressure, the $\beta'$ ordered phase coexists with $\alpha$ (disordered FCC) over a range of temperatures. How many degrees of freedom does this two-phase equilibrium have? If a third phase ($\gamma$) also becomes stable at a particular temperature, what happens?

$C = 2$, constant pressure. For $\alpha + \beta'$: $F = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$. One degree of freedom. Specifying the temperature fixes the compositions of both $\alpha$ and $\beta'$. The two-phase field is an area on the $T$ vs. composition diagram.

If a third phase $\gamma$ appears: $F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$. Zero degrees of freedom. This is an invariant reaction (a horizontal line on the diagram). It occurs at one specific temperature, and the compositions of all three phases are fixed. In the Cu-Zn system, such a reaction occurs at 558 °C: $\beta \rightarrow \alpha + \gamma$ (a eutectoid).

articles.title: Nucleation (Homogeneous & Heterogeneous)
articles.description: Deriving the critical radius and activation barrier for nucleation, comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous cases, with real undercooling data.
articles.intro: A phase transformation cannot begin unless a small region of the new phase first forms within the old one. This is nucleation, and it involves a competition between the volume free energy gained by forming the new phase and the surface energy penalty of creating an interface. The result is an energy barrier that governs when and where transformations start.
body: Consider a liquid metal cooled below its equilibrium melting temperature $T_m$. The liquid is now thermodynamically unstable: the solid has a lower Gibbs free energy. But forming a small particle of solid creates a new interface, and interfaces cost energy. For a spherical nucleus of radius $r$, the total free energy change is:

The first term is the volume free energy released (driving force), where $\Delta G_v$ is the free energy difference per unit volume between the liquid and solid. The second term is the surface energy penalty, where $\gamma$ is the interfacial energy between the solid nucleus and the surrounding liquid. The volume term scales as $r^3$; the surface term as $r^2$. At small $r$, the surface term wins. At large $r$, the volume term wins.
The critical radius $r^*$ is the size at which the free energy is at a maximum. Nuclei smaller than $r^*$ shrink and disappear; nuclei larger than $r^*$ grow spontaneously.

The activation barrier is found by substituting $r^*$ back into the expression for $\Delta G$:

Both $r^*$ and $\Delta G^*$ decrease as $\Delta G_v$ increases (larger undercooling). At the equilibrium melting point, $\Delta G_v = 0$, so $r^* \to \infty$ and nucleation is impossible. Nucleation requires undercooling.
The driving force $\Delta G_v$ depends on the undercooling $\Delta T = T_m - T$. Near $T_m$, it is well approximated by:
where $\Delta H_f$ is the latent heat of fusion per unit volume. This is a linear approximation, valid for moderate undercoolings. Substituting into the expression for $r^*$:
For pure copper: $T_m = 1358$ K, $\Delta H_f = 1.63 \times 10^9$ J/m$^3$, $\gamma_{SL} \approx 0.177$ J/m$^2$. At an undercooling of $\Delta T = 200$ K:
The critical nucleus is about 1.5 nm in radius, containing roughly 500 atoms. The barrier is:
This is a substantial barrier: about 87 times the thermal energy at the undercooling temperature. Homogeneous nucleation of copper requires significant undercooling.
The rate of nucleation (number of critical nuclei forming per unit volume per second) follows an Arrhenius form:

The pre-exponential factor $J_0$ accounts for the frequency of atomic attachment to the nucleus. Because $\Delta G^*$ appears in the exponent, the nucleation rate is extremely sensitive to undercooling. A small increase in $\Delta T$ dramatically increases $J$. Conversely, at very large undercoolings, atomic mobility drops (the liquid becomes viscous), and the nucleation rate decreases again. The net nucleation rate therefore passes through a maximum at an intermediate undercooling.

Homogeneous nucleation occurs in the bulk of the parent phase, with no assistance from pre-existing surfaces. It requires large undercoolings. Pure liquid nickel can be undercooled by 300 K below its melting point (1455 °C) in levitation experiments before it nucleates. Pure liquid iron, by about 295 K. These are heroic experiments using containerless processing to eliminate all foreign surfaces.
In ordinary casting, nucleation occurs at much smaller undercoolings (1 to 10 K) because it is heterogeneous.
A pre-existing surface (a mould wall, an oxide particle, a grain boundary) reduces the energy barrier. The nucleus forms as a spherical cap on the surface, and the activation barrier becomes:
where $\theta$ is the contact angle between the nucleus and the substrate, and:

This function ranges from 0 (perfect wetting, $\theta = 0$) to 1 (no wetting, $\theta = 180°$). For $\theta = 90°$, $f = 0.5$: the barrier is halved. For $\theta = 30°$, $f \approx 0.02$: the barrier is reduced by 98%.

The critical radius $r^*$ is unchanged; only the barrier height changes. The nucleus is smaller in volume (it is a cap, not a full sphere), but the radius of curvature at the critical point is the same as for homogeneous nucleation. What changes is the amount of new interface that must be created.

In aluminium casting, TiB₂ particles are added as grain refiners. They provide heterogeneous nucleation sites for $\alpha$-Al with very low contact angles. The result: instead of a few large grains nucleating at the mould wall, thousands of small grains nucleate throughout the melt, producing a fine equiaxed grain structure. A typical addition is 0.02 wt% Ti and 0.01 wt% B (as Al-5Ti-1B master alloy). The grain size drops from several millimetres to 200 $\mu$m or less.

Everything above applies to solid-state transformations too, with modifications. Precipitate nucleation in solids must additionally overcome elastic strain energy. If the precipitate has a different lattice parameter from the matrix, forming it compresses or stretches the surrounding material. The total free energy change becomes:

where $\Delta G_s$ is the strain energy per unit volume. This reduces the effective driving force and increases both $r^*$ and $\Delta G^*$. Coherent precipitates (with low interfacial energy $\gamma$ but significant strain $\Delta G_s$) nucleate more easily than incoherent ones (high $\gamma$, low $\Delta G_s$), which is why the precipitation sequence in most alloys starts with coherent metastable phases.

Pure liquid aluminium ($T_m = 933$ K, $\Delta H_f = 1.08 \times 10^9$ J/m$^3$, $\gamma_{SL} = 0.093$ J/m$^2$) is undercooled by 150 K. (a) Calculate the critical radius for homogeneous nucleation. (b) Estimate the number of atoms in the critical nucleus, given that the atomic volume of solid Al is $1.66 \times 10^{-29}$ m$^3$. (c) If heterogeneous nucleation occurs on a substrate with contact angle $\theta = 60°$, by what factor is the barrier reduced?
(a) The driving force per unit volume:

(b) Volume of the critical nucleus: $V^* = \frac{4}{3}\pi (1.07 \times 10^{-9})^3 = 5.1 \times 10^{-27}$ m$^3$. Number of atoms: $N = V^*/\Omega = 5.1 \times 10^{-27} / 1.66 \times 10^{-29} \approx 310$ atoms.
The barrier is reduced to 15.6% of the homogeneous value. This enormous reduction explains why heterogeneous nucleation dominates in practice.

articles.title: Growth Kinetics
articles.description: How new phases grow after nucleation: diffusion-controlled vs interface-controlled growth, the Johnson-Mehl-Avrami-Kolmogorov framework, and TTT diagrams.
articles.intro: Once a stable nucleus forms, it must grow. The rate of growth depends on whether atoms need to diffuse long distances to the growing interface, or whether the interface itself is the bottleneck. These two limiting cases, diffusion-controlled and interface-controlled growth, produce very different kinetics and very different microstructures.
body: If the new phase has the same composition as the parent (a polymorphic transformation), no long-range diffusion is needed. Growth is limited by the rate at which atoms can rearrange at the interface. The interface velocity is constant, independent of time:

The first exponential is the atomic mobility (Arrhenius). The bracketed term is the thermodynamic driving force, which vanishes at the equilibrium temperature and increases with undercooling. At small undercoolings, the driving force is small. At large undercoolings, the mobility is small. The growth rate peaks at an intermediate temperature.
Interface-controlled growth produces particles that grow linearly with time: $R \propto t$.

If the new phase differs in composition from the parent, solute must diffuse to or from the growing interface. This is the common case for precipitation, solidification of alloys, and most solid-state transformations.

Consider a spherical precipitate of composition $C_\beta$ growing in a matrix of nominal composition $C_0$, with the matrix-precipitate interface at local equilibrium (composition $C_i$, read from the phase diagram). The concentration gradient in the matrix ahead of the interface drives diffusion. As the precipitate grows, the diffusion field extends further into the matrix, and the gradient at the interface decreases. The classic result for a planar interface is:

The interface position advances as the square root of time. This parabolic growth law is characteristic of diffusion-controlled processes. For a spherical precipitate, the same scaling holds: $R \propto \sqrt{Dt}$.
The Zener approximation gives the growth rate of a spherical precipitate:
The growth rate is inversely proportional to $R$: large particles grow more slowly. The supersaturation ratio $(C_0 - C_i)/(C_\beta - C_i)$ captures the thermodynamic driving force.

Real transformations involve simultaneous nucleation and growth. The Johnson-Mehl-Avrami-Kolmogorov (JMAK) framework treats the overall transformation kinetics by accounting for nucleation rate, growth rate, and impingement of growing regions.
The fraction transformed $X$ as a function of time is:

Here $k$ is a rate constant that depends on nucleation and growth rates (and therefore on temperature), and $n$ is the Avrami exponent. The exponent contains information about the dimensionality of growth and the nucleation behaviour:
$n = 4$: constant nucleation rate, three-dimensional growth (e.g., equiaxed grains nucleating continuously in a melt).
$n = 3$: site-saturated nucleation (all nuclei present at $t = 0$), three-dimensional growth.
$n = 1$: site-saturated nucleation, one-dimensional (needle-like) growth or thickening of plates.
A log-log plot of $\ln[-\ln(1 - X)]$ vs $\ln t$ gives a straight line with slope $n$ and intercept $\ln k$. This is the standard way to extract JMAK parameters from experimental data.

The JMAK equation assumes spatially random nucleation, isotropic growth, and a single mechanism. Real transformations often violate these assumptions. Nucleation on grain boundaries is not random. Growth may be anisotropic (plates, needles). Multiple mechanisms may operate simultaneously (e.g., pearlite and bainite in steels). The JMAK equation remains a useful first approximation, but take the extracted $n$ values with appropriate scepticism when the assumptions are poor.

A time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram plots the start and finish of a transformation as a function of isothermal hold temperature. The classic example is the TTT diagram for a eutectoid steel (0.76 wt% C).

The diagram has a characteristic C-shape (or nose). At temperatures just below the eutectoid (727 °C), the driving force is small and transformation is slow. At very low temperatures, diffusion is sluggish and transformation is again slow. The fastest transformation occurs at the nose of the C-curve, around 540 °C for pearlite formation in a eutectoid steel.

Above the nose, the transformation product is coarse pearlite (wide lamellar spacing, lower hardness). Below the nose, fine pearlite forms. At still lower temperatures (below about 350 °C), a different transformation product appears: bainite, a non-lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite. Below the $M_s$ temperature (about 220 °C for a eutectoid steel), martensite forms athermally.

Continuous-cooling-transformation (CCT) diagrams are the practical counterpart of TTT diagrams. Most real heat treatments involve continuous cooling, not isothermal holds. The CCT curves are shifted to longer times and lower temperatures relative to the TTT curves, because the transformation has less time at each temperature.

The critical cooling rate is the minimum cooling rate that avoids the nose of the C-curve, producing a fully martensitic structure. For a plain 1080 steel, this is about 140 °C/s, requiring a water quench. For an alloyed steel like 4140 (with Cr and Mo), the C-curve is pushed to the right (longer times) and the critical cooling rate drops to about 8 °C/s, achievable with an oil quench. This is the entire purpose of adding alloying elements like Cr, Mo and Mn to steel: they retard diffusional transformations and make martensite easier to obtain.

The isothermal transformation of austenite to pearlite in a eutectoid steel at 600 °C follows JMAK kinetics with $n = 3$ and $k = 2.5 \times 10^{-6}$ s$^{-3}$. (a) Calculate the fraction transformed after 100 s. (b) How long does it take to reach 50% transformation? (c) What does $n = 3$ suggest about the nucleation and growth mechanism?

(c) $n = 3$ is consistent with site-saturated nucleation (all nuclei present at the start) with three-dimensional growth. This makes physical sense for pearlite at 600 °C: nucleation sites (grain boundaries, inclusions) are activated quickly, and the pearlite colonies then grow in three dimensions.

articles.title: Solidification & Microstructure
articles.description: How liquid metals freeze: constitutional supercooling, dendrite formation, columnar-to-equiaxed transition, and microsegregation.
articles.intro: Solidification is the transformation that shapes most metallic components. The microstructure it produces, whether columnar or equiaxed, coarse or fine, segregated or uniform, is set during freezing and is difficult to change afterward. Understanding what controls solidification microstructure is essential for anyone who designs or processes metals.
body: Most alloying elements have different solubilities in the liquid and solid phases. This is characterised by the partition coefficient:

where $C_S$ and $C_L$ are the solute concentrations in the solid and liquid at the interface, assuming local equilibrium. For most alloy systems, $k < 1$: the solid rejects solute into the liquid. Carbon in iron has $k \approx 0.17$. Silicon in aluminium has $k \approx 0.13$. Copper in aluminium has $k \approx 0.17$.

As the solid grows, solute piles up in the liquid ahead of the interface. In the steady state, a solute boundary layer develops with thickness $\delta \approx D/v$, where $D$ is the solute diffusivity in the liquid (typically $10^{-9}$ m$^2$/s) and $v$ is the interface velocity.

The solute enrichment ahead of the interface has a profound consequence. The liquidus temperature depends on composition: more solute means a lower liquidus. So the liquid immediately ahead of the interface, enriched in solute, has a lower equilibrium freezing temperature than the bulk liquid further away.

If the actual temperature gradient in the liquid is steep enough, the liquid everywhere ahead of the interface is above its local liquidus temperature, and the planar interface is stable. If the temperature gradient is shallow, a zone of liquid ahead of the interface is below its local liquidus; it is constitutionally supercooled. This supercooled zone is unstable. Any small protrusion of the solid into it finds itself in supercooled liquid and grows faster than its neighbours.
The criterion for a stable planar interface (no constitutional supercooling) is:

where $G$ is the temperature gradient in the liquid, $v$ is the growth velocity, $\Delta T_0 = T_L - T_S$ is the equilibrium freezing range of the alloy, and $D_L$ is the solute diffusivity in the liquid. The ratio $G/v$ is the key parameter. High $G/v$ (steep gradient, slow growth) stabilises a planar front. Low $G/v$ (shallow gradient, fast growth) destabilises it.

As $G/v$ decreases from the planar stability limit, the interface morphology progresses through: planar $\rightarrow$ cellular $\rightarrow$ columnar dendritic $\rightarrow$ equiaxed dendritic. Meanwhile, the product $G \times v$ (the cooling rate) controls the scale of the microstructure: higher cooling rates give finer structures. A casting solidifying at 1 K/s has dendrite arm spacings of hundreds of microns; laser-melted metal at $10^6$ K/s has spacings below 1 $\mu$m.

Once the planar interface breaks down, it does not become randomly rough. It develops a highly organised branching structure: a dendrite (from the Greek for tree). The primary arms grow along preferred crystallographic directions, which in cubic metals are the $\langle 100 \rangle$ directions. In aluminium, iron, nickel and copper, dendrites always grow along $\langle 100 \rangle$.

Why $\langle 100 \rangle$? This is set by the anisotropy of the solid-liquid interfacial energy. For FCC metals, the $\{100\}$ planes have slightly higher interfacial energy than the $\{111\}$ planes, and the resulting anisotropy, even though it is only a few percent, selects the growth direction. Without anisotropy, the interface would become unstable in a disordered way (seaweed morphology). Anisotropy organises the instability into a regular dendritic pattern.

Secondary arms branch from the primary stem, and tertiary arms from the secondaries. The secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) controls many mechanical properties because it sets the length scale of microsegregation. SDAS follows a power law with cooling rate:

where $B$ and $n$ are alloy-specific constants, and $n \approx 1/3$ for most aluminium and steel alloys. For Al-7Si (A356), the SDAS is about 50 $\mu$m at 1 K/s cooling rate, dropping to about 10 $\mu$m at 100 K/s.

In a typical casting, solidification begins at the mould wall, where the liquid is coldest. The temperature gradient points inward (toward the hotter liquid centre). Dendrites nucleate at the wall and grow inward, aligned with the heat flow direction. This produces a columnar zone of elongated grains.

Further from the wall, the temperature gradient decreases. If constitutional supercooling is sufficient, nucleation can occur in the bulk liquid ahead of the columnar front (on oxide particles, broken dendrite arms, or deliberately added grain refiners). These nuclei grow as equiaxed grains with no preferred orientation. The transition from columnar to equiaxed (CET) is one of the central problems in casting science.

The CET is promoted by: low temperature gradient (large mould, slow cooling), high solute content (larger constitutional supercooling), and abundant nucleation sites (grain refiners). It is suppressed by: high temperature gradient (directional solidification, thin sections) and low solute content (pure metals solidify entirely columnar).

Because the solid rejects solute ($k < 1$), the last liquid to solidify in the interdendritic regions is solute-rich. This is microsegregation. It is inevitable unless solid-state diffusion during freezing is fast enough to homogenise the solid (which requires very slow cooling).
The Scheil equation gives the composition of the solid as a function of fraction solidified $f_S$, assuming no diffusion in the solid and complete mixing in the liquid:

For Al-4.5 wt% Cu ($k = 0.17$): the first solid to form has $C_S = 0.17 \times 4.5 = 0.77$ wt% Cu. The last liquid, as $f_S \to 1$, is enriched to the eutectic composition (about 33 wt% Cu). The Scheil equation predicts that the last few percent of liquid reach the eutectic, even if the overall alloy composition is well below the eutectic. This is why most cast aluminium alloys contain some eutectic in the interdendritic regions, regardless of nominal composition.

Casting engineers control microstructure through three main levers: cooling rate (controls SDAS and grain size), alloy composition (controls constitutional supercooling and which phases form), and nucleating agents (control grain structure). In aluminium foundries, the standard recipe is Al-7Si-0.3Mg (A356), modified with 200 ppm strontium (to change the eutectic silicon from coarse plates to a fine fibrous morphology) and grain-refined with Al-5Ti-1B. In steel continuous casting, electromagnetic stirring is used to break up columnar dendrites and promote equiaxed grains in the centre of the billet.

An Al-3 wt% Cu alloy is solidified under Scheil conditions ($k = 0.17$, no solid diffusion, complete liquid mixing). (a) What is the copper concentration in the first solid to form? (b) At what fraction solid does the remaining liquid reach the eutectic composition of 33 wt% Cu? (c) What does this imply about the microstructure of the casting?
(a) First solid: $C_S = k C_0 = 0.17 \times 3 = 0.51$ wt% Cu.
(b) Set $C_L = 33$ wt% Cu. From the Scheil equation, $C_L = C_0 (1 - f_S)^{k-1}$:
The eutectic composition is reached at about 93.5% solid.

(c) About 6.5% of the alloy solidifies as eutectic (a mixture of $\alpha$-Al and Al₂Cu) in the interdendritic regions, even though the overall composition (3 wt% Cu) is far below the eutectic at 33 wt% Cu. This eutectic is visible in micrographs as a fine lamellar or divorced eutectic between the dendrite arms. It is a direct consequence of microsegregation during solidification.

articles.title: Spinodal Decomposition
articles.description: Phase separation without nucleation: the thermodynamics of uphill diffusion, the spinodal curve, and the Cahn-Hilliard equation.
articles.intro: Most phase transformations require nucleation: a localised fluctuation large enough to overcome an energy barrier. Spinodal decomposition is different. Inside the spinodal, the system is unstable to infinitesimal fluctuations, and decomposition proceeds spontaneously by uphill diffusion throughout the entire volume.
body: The free energy curve and the miscibility gap

Consider a binary system A-B at a temperature where the free energy of mixing curve $G(x)$ has a double-well shape: low at the A-rich and B-rich ends, with a hump in the middle. A homogeneous alloy with composition in the middle of the hump has a higher free energy than a mixture of two phases at compositions on either side. The system wants to separate.

The outer boundary of the two-phase region is the binodal (or miscibility gap), defined by the common tangent construction. Inside the binodal, phase separation is thermodynamically favourable. But how it occurs depends on where you are within the binodal.
The spinodal: where curvature changes sign
The spinodal is the locus of points where the second derivative of the free energy with respect to composition equals zero:

Between the two spinodal points, $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 < 0$: the free energy curve is concave. Outside the spinodal (but inside the binodal), $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 > 0$: the curve is convex.
This sign determines the kinetic pathway:

Between the binodal and spinodal (metastable region): $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 > 0$. Small composition fluctuations increase the free energy. The system is metastable, and decomposition requires nucleation (an activation barrier must be overcome).
Inside the spinodal (unstable region): $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 < 0$. Small composition fluctuations decrease the free energy. The system is unstable, and decomposition occurs spontaneously.

In normal (downhill) diffusion, atoms move from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration. Fick's first law gives a flux proportional to $-\partial C / \partial x$. But diffusion is actually driven by chemical potential gradients, not concentration gradients. The flux is:
J = -M \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial x} = -M \frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial x^2} \frac{\partial C}{\partial x}

where $M$ is the atomic mobility. The effective diffusion coefficient is $\tilde{D} = M (\partial^2 G / \partial x^2)$. When $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 > 0$, $\tilde{D} > 0$: ordinary downhill diffusion. When $\partial^2 G / \partial x^2 < 0$, $\tilde{D} < 0$: atoms diffuse from low concentration to high concentration. This is uphill diffusion, and it amplifies composition fluctuations rather than smoothing them out.

Inside the spinodal, there is no critical nucleus and no activation barrier. Every fluctuation, no matter how small, grows. This is fundamentally different from nucleation-and-growth, where only fluctuations exceeding the critical size survive. The result is a characteristic microstructure: interconnected, periodic composition modulations rather than discrete precipitate particles.
Cahn and Hilliard (1958) wrote down the governing equation for spinodal decomposition by adding a gradient energy term to the free energy. The composition evolves as:
\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = M \nabla^2 \left( \frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial C^2} C - 2\kappa \nabla^2 C \right)

The $\kappa$ term (the gradient energy coefficient) penalises sharp composition gradients, preventing the decomposition wavelength from shrinking to zero. The competition between the destabilising $\partial^2 G / \partial C^2 < 0$ (which drives decomposition) and the stabilising $\kappa$ term (which penalises short wavelengths) selects a dominant wavelength. This wavelength is typically 5 to 100 nm in metals.
A linear stability analysis of the Cahn-Hilliard equation shows that fluctuations with wavenumber $\beta$ grow exponentially with an amplification factor:
This sets the initial periodicity of the decomposition microstructure.

Spinodal decomposition produces a distinctive interconnected, labyrinthine microstructure in three dimensions. In the early stages, the composition modulation is approximately sinusoidal with a well-defined wavelength. As the decomposition progresses, the amplitudes grow until the equilibrium compositions are reached, and the modulations coarsen.

In the Cu-Ni-Fe system, spinodal decomposition at 625 °C produces periodic composition modulations along $\langle 100 \rangle$ with wavelengths of 10 to 30 nm. In Fe-Cr (the basis of ferritic stainless steels), spinodal decomposition of the $\alpha$ phase below 475 °C into Cr-rich $\alpha'$ and Fe-rich $\alpha$ causes '475 °C embrittlement', a serious service limitation for ferritic and duplex stainless steels. The decomposition wavelength is 2 to 5 nm in the early stages, making it invisible by optical microscopy but detectable by atom probe tomography.

Some alloys are designed to exploit spinodal decomposition. Alnico permanent magnets (Fe-Al-Ni-Co) achieve their magnetic hardness from spinodal decomposition into Fe-Co-rich ferromagnetic rods and Ni-Al-rich non-magnetic matrix, with a periodicity of about 30 nm aligned by a magnetic field applied during heat treatment. Cu-Ni-Sn spinodal alloys achieve high strength (yield stress above 1 GPa) from fine-scale composition modulations that impede dislocation motion.

A binary alloy system has a regular solution free energy of mixing $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = RT[x \ln x + (1-x) \ln(1-x)] + \Omega x(1-x)$, with $\Omega = 20$ kJ/mol. (a) Show that the spinodal condition $\partial^2 \Delta G_{\text{mix}} / \partial x^2 = 0$ gives $T_{\text{spinodal}} = \Omega x(1-x) \times 2 / R$. (b) Calculate the maximum spinodal temperature (the top of the spinodal dome). (c) Compare this to the critical temperature of the miscibility gap.
Setting this to zero: $RT / [x(1-x)] = 2\Omega$, so $T_{\text{spinodal}} = 2\Omega x(1-x)/R$.

(c) For a regular solution, the critical temperature of the miscibility gap (binodal) is $T_c = \Omega / (2R) = 20000 / (2 \times 8.314) = 1203$ K. The spinodal and binodal meet at the critical point. Below this temperature, the spinodal lies inside the binodal, and the two curves diverge with decreasing temperature.

articles.title: Precipitation & Age Hardening
articles.description: The precipitation sequence in Al-Cu alloys: GP zones, metastable phases, peak ageing, and the connection between microstructure and strength.
articles.intro: Age hardening was discovered accidentally by Alfred Wilm in 1906, when he noticed that a quenched aluminium-copper alloy became harder over time at room temperature. The mechanism, precipitation of fine second-phase particles that impede dislocation motion, took decades to understand. It remains one of the most important strengthening strategies in metallurgy.
body: Solution treatment: Heat the alloy into the single-phase $\alpha$ field. For Al-4 wt% Cu, this is above about 500 °C (the solvus temperature varies with composition). Hold long enough for all the copper to dissolve into the aluminium FCC lattice.

Quench: Cool rapidly to room temperature. The solid solution is now supersaturated: it contains more copper than the equilibrium solubility at room temperature (which is negligible, about 0.05 wt% at 25 °C). The quench traps excess vacancies, which accelerate subsequent diffusion.

Age: Hold at an elevated temperature (typically 120 to 190 °C for Al-Cu alloys) or at room temperature (natural ageing). Copper atoms diffuse and cluster into precipitates, progressively hardening the alloy.

The supersaturated solid solution (SSSS) does not jump directly to the equilibrium precipitate $\theta$ (Al₂Cu). Instead, it passes through a sequence of metastable phases, each more stable (lower free energy) than the last, but none of them the global equilibrium state:

GP zones (Guinier-Preston zones): Single-layer discs of copper atoms on $\{100\}$ planes of the aluminium matrix. They are fully coherent with the matrix (the copper atoms substitute directly onto Al lattice sites). Typical diameter: 3 to 10 nm. Thickness: one atom layer. They form at room temperature within hours to days. The coherency strain fields around GP zones interact with dislocations, producing the initial hardening.

$\theta''$: Multi-layer, ordered platelets on $\{100\}$, still fully coherent. Structure: two layers of Cu separated by three layers of Al, repeating. About 10 to 100 nm in diameter, 2 to 4 nm thick. $\theta''$ has the strongest coherency strains and is the principal strengthening phase in peak-aged Al-Cu.

$\theta'$: Tetragonal structure, semi-coherent (coherent on the broad face, incoherent on the edge). The broad face lies on $\{100\}_{\text{Al}}$ with a near-perfect lattice match, but the edge has misfit dislocations. Plates grow to hundreds of nanometres in diameter. Still a significant strengthener, but less effective per unit volume than $\theta''$.

$\theta$ (Al₂Cu): The equilibrium phase. Body-centred tetragonal ($a = 6.07$ A, $c = 4.87$ A). Fully incoherent with the matrix. Coarse particles, micron-scale. Provides almost no strengthening because dislocations bypass the particles rather than cutting through them. This is the overaged condition.

Nucleation is easier for phases with low interfacial energy. GP zones are fully coherent, so their interfacial energy is very low (of order 0.01 J/m$^2$, compared to $\sim$0.5 J/m$^2$ for incoherent $\theta$). The nucleation barrier scales as $\gamma^3 / (\Delta G_v)^2$, so even though $\theta$ has the larger driving force, GP zones have a vastly smaller barrier. They nucleate first, in enormous numbers.

Each subsequent phase in the sequence has a lower free energy but a higher nucleation barrier. The system cascades through metastable states, each one easier to reach from its predecessor than jumping directly to $\theta$. This is Ostwald's step rule in action.
Hardness plotted against ageing time (at fixed temperature) shows a characteristic peak:
Initially, hardness rises as GP zones and $\theta''$ form. The alloy is underaged.

At peak ageing, the optimum distribution of fine, coherent precipitates is achieved. For Al-4 wt% Cu aged at 130 °C, peak hardness is about 130 HV, reached after roughly 100 hours. At 190 °C, peak hardness is slightly lower (about 120 HV) but reached in just 5 to 10 hours.
Beyond the peak, precipitates coarsen ($\theta'' \to \theta' \to \theta$), the interparticle spacing increases, and hardness falls. The alloy is overaged.

The trade-off is clear. Higher ageing temperature reaches the peak faster but produces a lower peak hardness (because the precipitates coarsen more readily). Lower ageing temperature gives higher peak hardness but takes longer to reach. Industrial practice selects the ageing temperature and time based on the required properties and production throughput.
Fine precipitates strengthen the alloy by interacting with dislocations. Two mechanisms operate:

Precipitate shearing (for small, coherent particles): The dislocation cuts through the precipitate. The resistance comes from the energy of creating new precipitate-matrix interface, the disruption of chemical order within the precipitate, and the coherency strain fields. Shearing stress increases with precipitate size (up to a point).

Orowan bypassing (for large, incoherent particles): The dislocation cannot cut through the particle. Instead it bows between adjacent particles, leaving a dislocation loop around each one. The Orowan stress is:
where $G$ is the shear modulus, $b$ the Burgers vector, and $L$ the interparticle spacing. As particles coarsen, $L$ increases and the stress decreases. This is why overageing softens the alloy.

Peak hardness occurs at the crossover between shearing and bypassing, where the precipitates are large enough to strongly resist shearing but small enough that Orowan bypassing is still expensive. For Al-Cu, this corresponds to $\theta''$ plates about 50 to 100 nm in diameter.

Al-Cu is the textbook case, but commercial age-hardening alloys use more complex chemistries. 2024 (Al-4.4Cu-1.5Mg) strengthens by S-phase (Al₂CuMg) and $\theta'$ precipitates. 6061 (Al-1.0Mg-0.6Si) uses $\beta''$ (Mg₅Si₆) needles along $\langle 100 \rangle_{\text{Al}}$. 7075 (Al-5.6Zn-2.5Mg-1.6Cu) uses $\eta'$ (MgZn₂) precipitates and is the strongest common aluminium alloy, reaching 230 HV in the T6 temper. Nickel superalloys (e.g., Inconel 718) are age-hardened by $\gamma'$ (Ni₃Al) and $\gamma''$ (Ni₃Nb), operating on the same principles at much higher temperatures.

An Al-4 wt% Cu alloy is solution-treated at 540 °C and quenched. It is then aged at 150 °C. (a) Why must the alloy be quenched rather than slowly cooled? (b) The equilibrium precipitate is $\theta$ (Al₂Cu), but GP zones form first. Explain why, in terms of nucleation barriers. (c) If the alloy is aged for too long, the hardness drops below its peak value. Explain the mechanism.

(a) Slow cooling allows copper to precipitate out along the equilibrium pathway, forming coarse, widely spaced $\theta$ particles that provide no significant strengthening. Quenching retains the copper in supersaturated solid solution, providing the maximum driving force for subsequent precipitation of fine, closely spaced metastable phases. Quenching also traps excess vacancies, which accelerate copper diffusion at the ageing temperature.

(b) GP zones are fully coherent with the Al matrix, so the GP zone-matrix interfacial energy is very low (approximately 0.01 J/m$^2$). The equilibrium $\theta$ phase is incoherent, with a much higher interfacial energy (approximately 0.5 J/m$^2$). The nucleation barrier $\Delta G^* \propto \gamma^3 / (\Delta G_v)^2$, so even though $\theta$ has a larger driving force ($\Delta G_v$), the $\gamma^3$ term overwhelmingly favours GP zone nucleation. GP zones nucleate first because they have a much smaller barrier, despite being metastable.

(c) With prolonged ageing, the precipitates evolve from $\theta''$ through $\theta'$ to $\theta$ and coarsen (Ostwald ripening: large particles grow at the expense of small ones). The interparticle spacing $L$ increases, reducing the Orowan bypassing stress $\tau \propto 1/L$. The precipitates also lose coherency, reducing the coherency-strain contribution to strengthening. Both effects lower the hardness. This is overageing.

articles.title: Martensitic Transformations
articles.description: Diffusionless transformations: the athermal nature of martensite, the Ms temperature, crystallography, and the shape memory effect.
articles.intro: Martensite is the product of a transformation that requires no diffusion. Atoms move cooperatively, by less than one interatomic spacing each, in a military rather than civilian manner. The result is a new crystal structure formed at the speed of sound, with a characteristic plate or lath morphology that has no time to reach equilibrium.
body: Most solid-state phase transformations involve diffusion: atoms jump one at a time across an interface, sorting themselves by species. Martensitic transformations are the opposite. Every atom moves simultaneously, by a fraction of an interatomic distance, in a coordinated shear. There is no change in composition. The transformation is so fast (interface velocities approach 1000 m/s, close to the speed of sound in the material) that diffusion has no time to occur.

The parent phase (austenite, in steels) and the product phase (martensite) have the same composition but different crystal structures. In carbon steels, austenite is FCC and martensite is BCT (body-centred tetragonal), with carbon atoms trapped in octahedral interstitial sites that were large enough in the FCC structure but are too small in the BCC-derived structure. The resulting lattice distortion is what makes martensite hard.

Martensitic transformations are athermal: the amount of martensite formed depends on the temperature reached, not on the time held at that temperature. Cool to a given temperature below $M_s$ and a certain fraction transforms. Hold there for hours and no more forms. Cool further and more transforms. This is fundamentally different from diffusional transformations, where fraction transformed increases with time at constant temperature (JMAK kinetics).
The start temperature $M_s$ is the temperature at which martensite first appears on cooling. For a plain carbon steel:

All common alloying elements depress $M_s$. A eutectoid steel (0.76 wt% C) has $M_s \approx 220$ °C. A high-carbon steel with 1.2 wt% C has $M_s \approx 30$ °C, meaning much of the austenite may not transform to martensite even on quenching to room temperature: the untransformed austenite is retained austenite.
The fraction of martensite formed follows the Koistinen-Marburger equation:

where $\alpha \approx 0.011$ °C$^{-1}$ for many steels. At $T = M_s - 200$ °C, $f_M = 1 - \exp(-2.2) \approx 0.89$; about 89% martensite. The $M_f$ temperature (where transformation is essentially complete, say 95%) is typically $M_s - 270$ °C.

The Bain correspondence describes the lattice distortion that converts FCC austenite to BCT martensite. It is a compression of about 17% along one $\langle 001 \rangle_{\gamma}$ axis and an expansion of about 12% in the perpendicular plane. But the Bain strain alone would produce a shape change so large that the surrounding austenite could not accommodate it elastically.

In reality, the shape change is reduced by a lattice-invariant deformation: either slip (in lath martensite, found in low-carbon steels) or twinning (in plate martensite, found in high-carbon steels and non-ferrous alloys). The combination of the Bain strain and the lattice-invariant deformation produces an invariant plane strain: the habit plane between martensite and austenite is undistorted and unrotated. This is the central result of the phenomenological theory of martensite crystallography (PTMC), developed by Wechsler, Lieberman and Read, and independently by Bowles and Mackenzie, in the 1950s.

In low-carbon steels ($< 0.6$ wt% C), martensite forms as laths grouped in packets and blocks within prior austenite grains. The habit plane is near $\{557\}_\gamma$. In high-carbon steels ($> 1.0$ wt% C), martensite forms as individual plates with a midrib of fine transformation twins. The habit plane is near $\{259\}_\gamma$.

The hardness of martensite in steels comes primarily from carbon in solid solution. The carbon atoms occupy octahedral interstitial sites that are tetragonally distorted in the BCT lattice. This creates strong elastic interactions with dislocations (solid-solution hardening). The tetragonality ratio $c/a$ increases linearly with carbon content:
At 0.8 wt% C, $c/a \approx 1.036$. At 0.2 wt% C, $c/a \approx 1.009$: the structure is nearly cubic.

For a eutectoid steel, as-quenched martensite has a hardness of about 65 HRC (approximately 840 HV). A 0.20 wt% C steel produces martensite of about 45 HRC (450 HV). The relationship between carbon content and martensite hardness is approximately linear up to about 0.6 wt% C, then flattens because retained austenite becomes significant.

As-quenched martensite is hard but brittle. Tempering (reheating to 150 to 650 °C) allows carbon to diffuse out of the BCT lattice and form fine carbide particles ($\epsilon$-carbide at low temperatures, cementite at higher temperatures). The tetragonality is relieved, ductility and toughness improve, and hardness decreases. The classic trade-off: temper at 200 °C for maximum hardness with some ductility (spring steels, cutting tools); temper at 550 to 650 °C for maximum toughness with moderate strength (structural steels, shafts).
Martensitic transformations are not limited to the FCC $\to$ BCT transformation in steels. They occur in many alloy systems:
Titanium alloys: $\beta$ (BCC) $\to$ $\alpha'$ (HCP) on quenching. Ti-6Al-4V forms $\alpha'$ martensite when water-quenched from above the $\beta$-transus (about 995 °C).
Cobalt: FCC $\to$ HCP on cooling through 422 °C. This is why pure cobalt is difficult to cold-work: the martensitic transformation produces planar defects.
Zirconia (ZrO₂): tetragonal $\to$ monoclinic on cooling, with a 4% volume expansion. This is a problem in nuclear fuel cladding but is exploited in transformation-toughened ceramics.

In certain alloys, the martensitic transformation is thermoelastic: the martensite plates form and shrink continuously with temperature, and the transformation is fully reversible. Nickel-titanium (Nitinol, near-equiatomic NiTi) is the classic example. The transformation is from a B2 (ordered BCC) parent phase to a monoclinic B19' martensite, with $M_s$ tuneable from $-100$ to $+100$ °C by adjusting composition and thermomechanical processing.

The shape memory effect works as follows: deform the martensite (below $M_s$) by detwinning, converting one twin variant to another. The macroscopic shape changes, but the crystal structure remains martensite. On heating above $A_f$ (the austenite finish temperature), the martensite reverts to austenite, and the original shape is recovered. The shape change can be up to 8% strain in NiTi, recovered completely on heating. This is used in medical stents, actuators, and pipe couplings.

Superelasticity (pseudoelasticity) is the related effect observed above $A_f$: apply a stress, and stress-induced martensite forms; release the stress, and it reverts to austenite. NiTi wires can recover up to 8% strain elastically by this mechanism, compared to 0.2% for conventional metals. Orthodontic archwires exploit this: they apply a nearly constant force over a large range of deflection.

A plain carbon steel contains 0.45 wt% C and 0.75 wt% Mn. (a) Estimate the $M_s$ temperature. (b) Calculate the fraction of martensite at room temperature (25 °C) using the Koistinen-Marburger equation with $\alpha = 0.011$ °C$^{-1}$. (c) Why does carbon depress $M_s$?
About 96% martensite. The remaining 4% is retained austenite.

(c) Carbon stabilises austenite (it lowers the FCC-to-BCC free energy difference) and increases the strain energy associated with the martensitic transformation (because the tetragonal distortion of the BCT product is proportional to carbon content). Both effects mean a lower temperature is needed before the driving force overcomes the resistance to transformation.

articles.title: Order-Disorder Transitions
articles.description: Long-range and short-range order, the Bragg-Williams model, superlattice reflections, and real examples in Cu-Au and Cu-Zn.
articles.intro: In a disordered alloy, atoms occupy lattice sites at random. In an ordered alloy, they adopt a periodic arrangement on a superlattice. The transition between these states, driven by the balance between ordering enthalpy and configurational entropy, changes mechanical properties, diffraction patterns, and physical behaviour.
body: Consider a binary alloy A-B on a lattice where each site has $z$ nearest neighbours. In a perfectly random (disordered) solid solution, the probability of finding a B atom on any site equals the mole fraction $x_B$, regardless of what is on the neighbouring sites. In a perfectly ordered structure, A and B atoms segregate onto distinct sublattices in a regular pattern.
Order is quantified by the long-range order parameter $S$:
where $p_A^\alpha$ is the fraction of $\alpha$-sublattice sites occupied by A atoms. $S = 1$ for perfect order; $S = 0$ for complete disorder. Intermediate values represent partial order.

The Cu-Au system shows ordering at two compositions. Cu₃Au (75 at% Cu) orders below 390 °C into the L1₂ structure: gold atoms sit on the corner sites and copper atoms on the face centres of an FCC-derived superlattice. CuAu (50 at%) orders below 410 °C into the L1₀ structure: alternating layers of pure Cu and pure Au along one $\langle 001 \rangle$ direction, producing a tetragonal distortion ($c/a \approx 0.92$).

The ordering transformation in Cu₃Au is first-order: $S$ jumps discontinuously from 0 to about 0.8 at the critical temperature. There is latent heat (about 2.1 kJ/mol) and a sharp change in resistivity. The CuAu ordering is also first-order, with a more complex two-stage process involving CuAu-I (ordered tetragonal) and CuAu-II (a long-period antiphase domain structure).
The Bragg-Williams model predicts the critical temperature for ordering by balancing the enthalpy of ordering against the entropy of mixing.

Even above the critical temperature, the alloy is not perfectly random. Local correlations persist: unlike neighbours remain slightly more probable than random statistics would predict. This is short-range order (SRO). It is quantified by the Warren-Cowley SRO parameter:

where $p_{AB}^{(i)}$ is the probability of finding a B atom in the $i$-th coordination shell of an A atom. $\alpha_i = 0$ for random; $\alpha_i < 0$ for ordering (more AB pairs than random); $\alpha_i > 0$ for clustering (fewer AB pairs than random).

SRO produces diffuse scattering in diffraction experiments: broad humps in the background between the Bragg peaks. Long-range order produces sharp superlattice reflections at positions forbidden by the disordered structure. The appearance of superlattice reflections (e.g., the 100 and 110 peaks in Cu₃Au, which are absent in disordered FCC) is the definitive signature of long-range ordering.

The $\beta$-brass phase (near CuZn, 50 at% Zn) has a BCC-based structure. Above 468 °C, it is disordered BCC (A2). Below 468 °C, it orders into the B2 (CsCl) structure: Cu on corner sites, Zn on body-centre sites (or vice versa). This is the $\beta \to \beta'$ transition.

Unlike Cu₃Au, the $\beta$-brass ordering transition is second-order (or very weakly first-order): $S$ decreases continuously to zero at $T_c$, with no discontinuous jump and no latent heat. The heat capacity shows a lambda-shaped peak at $T_c$, characteristic of a continuous phase transition. This difference, first-order in Cu₃Au and second-order in $\beta$-brass, is a consequence of the different symmetries of the ordered structures.

Mechanical: Ordered alloys are generally harder and more brittle than their disordered counterparts. Dislocations in an ordered structure must travel in pairs (superdislocations), with an antiphase boundary (APB) between them. The APB energy provides an additional barrier to dislocation motion. The yield stress of Ni₃Al ($\gamma'$) actually increases with temperature up to about 700 °C (the anomalous yield stress effect), because thermally activated cross-slip of screw superdislocations locks them on $\{100\}$ planes.
Electrical: Ordering reduces electrical resistivity because the periodic arrangement of atoms reduces electron scattering. In Cu₃Au, the resistivity drops by about 50% on ordering.

Magnetic: In Fe-Al alloys, the transition from disordered A2 to ordered B2 to further-ordered D0₃ changes the magnetic behaviour, because the magnetic exchange interactions depend on the local atomic environment.

When a disordered alloy is cooled below $T_c$, ordered domains nucleate at many sites. Each domain has the same ordered structure but may be out of phase with its neighbours (e.g., in one domain, Cu is on corners and Au on face centres; in the adjacent domain, the assignment is reversed). The boundaries between these domains are antiphase boundaries (APBs). APBs are visible in TEM as additional contrast in dark-field images taken using superlattice reflections.

The APB energy in Cu₃Au is about 40 mJ/m$^2$. In Ni₃Al it is about 110 mJ/m$^2$, which is why $\gamma'$ precipitates in nickel superalloys are such effective strengtheners: the high APB energy forces superdislocations to travel in tightly bound pairs, making plastic deformation difficult.
Why ordering matters for alloy design

Ordering is not an academic curiosity. The $\gamma'$ (Ni₃Al, L1₂) precipitate phase in nickel-base superalloys derives its extraordinary high-temperature strength from the ordered structure and the anomalous yield stress effect. The entire gas turbine industry depends on it. Fe-Si transformer steels rely on B2/D0₃ ordering to minimise hysteresis losses. CoPt and FePt ordered alloys are candidates for next-generation magnetic recording media because of their extremely high magnetocrystalline anisotropy.

In $\beta$-brass (CuZn), the B2 ordered structure has Cu on corner sites and Zn on body-centre sites of a BCC lattice. (a) What superlattice reflections appear in the ordered state that are absent in the disordered A2 structure? (b) The critical temperature is 468 °C. Using the Bragg-Williams result $T_c = -zW/(2k_B)$ with $z = 8$ (BCC), estimate the ordering energy $|W|$ per bond. (c) Is the transition first-order or second-order, and what experimental evidence distinguishes them?

(a) In disordered BCC (A2), the structure factor vanishes for reflections with $h + k + l$ = odd (e.g., 100, 111, 210). In the B2 ordered structure, the two sublattices have different average scattering factors, so these reflections are no longer forbidden. The superlattice reflections are those with $h + k + l$ = odd. The 100 and 111 reflections are the most commonly used to characterise B2 ordering.

(c) The $\beta$-brass ordering is second-order (or very nearly so). The order parameter $S$ decreases continuously to zero at $T_c$, with no discontinuous jump. Experimentally, the evidence is: (i) no latent heat at $T_c$ (only a lambda anomaly in the heat capacity), (ii) the intensity of the superlattice reflections decreases continuously to zero as $T \to T_c$ from below, and (iii) there is no two-phase coexistence region on the phase diagram (the transition occurs at a single line, not across a two-phase field).
